incidents.title: Server 1 is overloaded
incidents.brief: Three app servers are live, but 90% of traffic still routes to Server 1.
incidents.constraint: The other servers are almost idle.
incidents.question: What is the root cause?

choices.label: Deploy Layer 7 Reverse Proxy (Nginx/HAProxy) with Least-Connections balancing
choices.resultBody: The Layer 7 load balancer distributes incoming requests evenly across the server fleet, stabilizing CPU utilization across all nodes.

choices.label: Assume backend database lock contention and scale DB instance size
choices.resultBody: Scaling the database does not address compute traffic skew. Server 1 remains pegged at 100% CPU while Server 2 and 3 sit completely idle.

choices.label: Rely solely on Client-Side DNS Round Robin without health checks or session awareness
choices.resultBody: Client DNS caching (ISPs and browsers) binds thousands of users to a single IP address for hours, preserving the traffic imbalance.

incidents.title: One server dies
incidents.brief: An instance fails in the middle of a traffic burst and requests start failing immediately.
incidents.constraint: The remaining servers are healthy but not all traffic is rerouted.
incidents.question: How do you route around the failure?

choices.label: Configure Active Health Checks with automatic dead-node eviction (<3s failover)
choices.resultBody: The load balancer detects failed HTTP health checks and immediately routes traffic away from the dead node to healthy surviving instances.

choices.label: Manually update DNS A-records in Route53 whenever an app node crashes
choices.resultBody: Manual DNS updates take minutes to execute, and downstream DNS resolver TTL caching keeps sending traffic to the crashed server for up to an hour.

choices.label: Rely on client retries to eventually hit surviving nodes without server-side failover
choices.resultBody: Without automated server-side failover, 1 in every 3 requests continues hitting the dead node, generating waves of 502 Bad Gateway errors.

incidents.title: Mobile clients bypass the public endpoint
incidents.brief: The app has two servers, but mobile traffic is still pointed at the old host directly.
incidents.constraint: The app layer is horizontally scaled but not reachable through the load balancer.
incidents.question: What completes the fix?

choices.label: Consolidate public ingress behind Anycast BGP VIP routed through Load Balancer fleet
choices.resultBody: Clients connect to a single resilient VIP, completely decoupling client devices from internal server topology and lifecycle.

choices.label: Publish hardcoded secondary IP addresses in client mobile app binaries
choices.resultBody: Hardcoding server IP addresses inside mobile apps requires an app store update whenever infrastructure changes, creating permanent failure paths for older app versions.

choices.label: Embed client-side round-robin IP rotation inside mobile app code
choices.resultTitle: Unsynchronized Balancing & DDoS on Single Node
choices.resultBody: Client-side rotation lacks centralized visibility into backend server health, easily sending traffic storms into degraded nodes.

incidents.title: Uneven traffic after a deployment
incidents.brief: A new version is deployed to two servers, but one receives 68% of the traffic.
incidents.constraint: The balancing policy is not consistent and one node gets more than its share.
incidents.question: What is the immediate design problem?

choices.label: Switch routing algorithm from Round Robin to Least Requests with Slow-Start warmup
choices.resultBody: Least-Requests routing dynamically accounts for request processing duration, sending new requests only to servers with available capacity.

choices.label: Blame application cache misses for uneven traffic distribution across identical pods
choices.resultBody: Adding caching layers does not fix the root cause of an ingress router blindly dumping requests onto already saturated servers.

choices.label: Attempt database schema migration to fix uneven web worker CPU distribution
choices.resultBody: Database schema restructuring has zero effect on Layer 7 HTTP connection routing, introducing downtime risk without fixing server load skew.

incidents.title: Latency climbs after an app restart
incidents.brief: One app server is restarted and the traffic is still mostly directed to the old instance.
incidents.constraint: Healthy nodes are available but get little traffic.
incidents.question: What keeps the system unhealthy?

choices.label: Enable Weighted Slow-Start ramp-up to allow JVM/JIT and connection pools to warm up gradually
choices.resultBody: Slow-Start gently increases traffic weighting over 60 seconds, allowing JIT compilation and database pools to initialize without crashing.

choices.label: Blame asynchronous message broker backlog for synchronous HTTP handshake latency
choices.resultBody: Investigating queue backlogs wastes critical triage time while newly restarted application containers are crushed by full traffic loads before warming up.

choices.label: Assume file system disk corruption on newly restarted container images
choices.resultBody: Container images are immutable and verify checksums; rebuilding disk images does not solve cold-start CPU spikes.

incidents.title: All traffic hits one edge instance
incidents.brief: A single edge service is the main public door, but the remaining edges are not in rotation.
incidents.constraint: The app is scaled yet not balanced.
incidents.question: What is the best fix?

choices.label: Implement Consistent Hashing with Virtual Nodes across edge ingress proxies
choices.resultBody: Virtual nodes on the hash ring distribute client connections uniformly across the edge fleet, eliminating traffic hot-spotting.

choices.label: Provision another database replica to resolve edge traffic concentration
choices.resultBody: Adding database replicas does not alter ingress reverse proxy traffic routing, leaving the edge node saturated.

choices.label: Deploy CDN edge for dynamic websocket traffic that cannot be cached at the edge
choices.resultBody: CDNs cannot cache dynamic bi-directional WebSocket connections, so all socket traffic still funnels to the single un-balanced origin node.

incidents.title: A region fails but no traffic shift happens
incidents.brief: A regional app server crashes, yet clients continue hitting the bad endpoint for a long time.
incidents.constraint: There is a health check gap.
incidents.question: Which property should the distribution layer provide?

choices.label: Configure Global Server Load Balancing (GSLB) with automated GeoDNS and health probes
choices.resultBody: GSLB probes detect regional datacenter impairment and dynamically update DNS routing to send global traffic to healthy secondary regions.

choices.label: Rely on client-side HTTP retries across transatlantic links without regional DNS failover
choices.resultBody: If an entire region's power or network link fails, clients in that geography cannot connect at all, making retries futile without DNS traffic shifting.

choices.label: Hardcode static backup IP without active cross-region health verification
choices.resultBody: Failing over to a static IP without health verification risks dumping all global traffic into an unprovisioned or equally degraded secondary region.

incidents.title: Traffic spins between two servers
incidents.brief: A two-node system alternates latency spikes even though the nodes are healthy.
incidents.constraint: The routing algorithm is not aware of node health and session stickiness is weak.
incidents.question: What should be improved?

choices.label: Enable Sticky Sessions (Session Affinity via Cookie) with consistent hash fallbacks
choices.resultBody: Cookie-based session affinity ensures stateful shopping carts and auth sessions remain anchored to the correct backend node.

choices.label: Normalize relational database tables hoping it fixes cross-server session loss
choices.resultBody: Database table normalization does not prevent a stateless load balancer from alternating user requests between different server memories.

choices.label: Increase DNS TTL to 24 hours to freeze client route decisions
choices.resultBody: High DNS TTLs freeze client routing at ISP levels, preventing rapid failover during incidents while failing to solve multi-server load skew.

incidents.title: Cascading failures after one crash
incidents.brief: During a moderate surge, one node dies and the rest absorb too much traffic until they also fail.
incidents.constraint: The load balancer had no failover policy for partial failure.
incidents.question: What design decision prevents this pattern?

choices.label: Deploy Load Balancer with Shed-Load Rate Limiting and Circuit Breaker to prevent thundering herd
choices.resultBody: Load shedding returns immediate 429/503 responses to excess traffic, protecting surviving servers from being overwhelmed when one node dies.

choices.label: Increase CPU on the first node without load balancing, leaving it as a single point of failure
choices.resultBody: Vertical scaling increases the blast radius when that single node crashes, causing complete system failure.

choices.label: Increase connection timeouts on the load balancer, cascading thread exhaustion across all nodes
choices.resultBody: Holding dead connections open exhausts connection pools and thread workers across all surviving servers, accelerating cascading collapse.

incidents.title: Traffic is uneven by geography
incidents.brief: Users in Europe are routed to one node while Asia goes to another, and one node is overloaded.
incidents.constraint: The balancing layer is not aware of region or health.
incidents.question: What is the correct balancing principle?

choices.label: Deploy Latency-Based GeoDNS Routing with health-monitored regional edge points of presence
choices.resultBody: GeoDNS routes users to the geographically closest datacenter with sub-20ms latency, balancing load evenly across global points of presence.

choices.label: Force global users through simple round-robin, routing European users to Tokyo servers
choices.resultBody: Naive round-robin routes users to random continents, incurring massive speed-of-light fiber latency penalties.

choices.label: Manually prompt users to select their region on every page load with cookies
choices.resultBody: Manual geographic selection causes 25% user drop-off and fails to redirect traffic dynamically when a chosen region experiences an outage.

incidents.title: gRPC clients pin to one pod
incidents.brief: A gRPC client pool opens long-lived connections and 80% of RPCs stay on the first pod.
incidents.constraint: The balancer only sees connection count, not RPC rate.
incidents.question: What restores even RPC distribution?

choices.label: Fresh reads
choices.resultBody: Balance at request level or refresh backends so long-lived connections do not pin load.

choices.label: Add more database
choices.resultBody: Traffic never left the hot node.

choices.label: Increase HTTP timeouts
choices.resultBody: Increase HTTP timeouts

incidents.title: Health checks pass on a dying node
incidents.brief: A node answers /health in 5ms but its request queue is 12 seconds deep.
incidents.constraint: The probe does not measure real work capacity.
incidents.question: What should the balancer use instead?

choices.label: Health checks
choices.resultBody: Health checks that include queue depth, error rate, or dependency readiness.

choices.label: Ping operating system
choices.resultBody: Traffic never left the hot node.

choices.label: Disable health checks
choices.resultBody: Disable health checks

incidents.title: Canary takes all production traffic
incidents.brief: A 5% canary is deployed, but weighted routing is misconfigured and the canary receives 100%.
incidents.constraint: The canary has far less capacity than the stable pool.
incidents.question: What did the balancing layer fail to do?

choices.label: Load balancer
choices.resultBody: Honor traffic weights so only a small share reaches the canary.

choices.label: Delete stable pool
choices.resultBody: Traffic never left the hot node.

choices.label: Increase canary CPU
choices.resultBody: Increase canary CPU after the spike

incidents.title: Least-connections prefers a slow node
incidents.brief: A slow instance holds connections longer, so least-connections keeps sending it more work.
incidents.constraint: Connection count is a poor proxy for remaining capacity.
incidents.question: How should routing adapt?

choices.label: Load balancer
choices.resultBody: Use latency-aware or utilization-aware balancing, not connection count alone.

choices.label: Always use source-IP
choices.resultBody: Traffic never left the hot node.

choices.label: Turn off fast
choices.resultBody: Turn off the fast nodes

incidents.title: Internal services skip the mesh
incidents.brief: Public traffic is balanced, but service-to-service calls go to hardcoded IPs.
incidents.constraint: One internal host becomes a hidden hotspot.
incidents.question: What completes the architecture?

choices.label: Load balancer
choices.resultBody: Send east-west traffic through a balancer or service mesh with health-aware routing.

choices.label: Hardcode second IP
choices.resultBody: Traffic never left the hot node.

choices.label: Add CDN front
choices.resultBody: Add a CDN in front of internal RPCs

incidents.title: Draining a node still receives writes
incidents.brief: An instance is marked for deploy, but new requests keep landing on it until it is killed.
incidents.constraint: The balancer has no connection-drain or weight-zero path.
incidents.question: What should happen before shutdown?

choices.label: Load balancer
choices.resultBody: Take the node out of rotation, drain in-flight work, then stop the process.

choices.label: Kill process immediately
choices.resultBody: Traffic never left the hot node.

choices.label: Lower DNS TTL
choices.resultBody: Lower DNS TTL only

incidents.title: Layer-4 balancer hides HTTP errors
incidents.brief: TCP health checks stay green while the app returns 503 on every request.
incidents.constraint: The balancer only knows the port is open.
incidents.question: What check is missing?

choices.label: Health checks
choices.resultBody: Application-level health checks that fail when the service cannot serve correctly.

choices.label: More TCP connections
choices.resultBody: Traffic never left the hot node.

choices.label: A larger SYN
choices.resultBody: A larger SYN backlog

incidents.title: Sticky sessions after node loss
incidents.brief: A node dies and users bound to it get errors until their sticky cookie expires.
incidents.constraint: Affinity outlives the backend.
incidents.question: How should the balancer behave?

choices.label: Load balancer
choices.resultBody: Drop affinity for dead targets and reassign those users to healthy nodes.

choices.label: Keep sending them
choices.resultBody: Traffic never left the hot node.

choices.label: Force all users
choices.resultBody: Force all users onto one remaining node forever

incidents.title: Burst of retries overwhelms survivors
incidents.brief: Clients retry failed calls and the remaining two nodes receive 3x traffic instantly.
incidents.constraint: The balancer has no retry budget or overload shed.
incidents.question: What protection belongs at the distribution layer?

choices.label: Load balancer
choices.resultBody: Shed load, cap retries, and keep enough healthy capacity before amplifying traffic.

choices.label: Retry every failure
choices.resultBody: Traffic never left the hot node.

choices.label: Disable remaining nodes
choices.resultBody: Disable the remaining nodes

incidents.title: Anycast edge sends all packets to one PoP
incidents.brief: An Anycast VIP is announced from three PoPs, but one PoP attracts almost all users.
incidents.constraint: Routing is based on BGP, not backend health.
incidents.question: What should you add behind the VIP?

choices.label: Health checks
choices.resultBody: Local load balancing with health checks inside each PoP, plus withdraw unhealthy announcements.

choices.label: A single origin
choices.resultBody: Traffic never left the hot node.

choices.label: Manual user assignment
choices.resultBody: Manual user assignment by country code only
